opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Yesterday, my son asked me a question that honestly did not surprise me. He wondered whether belief in God is simply the result of not having enough information. That maybe previous generations turned to prayer and faith because they lacked the resources and knowledge now available to us. And if anyone is wavering in belief, I think at some point they inevitably wrestle with this exact question.
Then today comes the Ascension. The apostles stand there watching Christ ascend, and the angels simply say:
 “This Jesus who has been taken up from you into heaven will return in the same way as you have seen him going into heaven.” No timeline. No explanation. Just the statement.

And what struck me is that the apostles themselves probably did not fully understand what they were witnessing either. These were not men simply “filling gaps” in knowledge. The Gospels repeatedly show confusion, doubt, fear, misunderstanding, even after the resurrection itself. Thomas demands proof. Others still question. Yet they continue following something they cannot fully explain.

Then in Ephesians comes the line: “May the eyes of your hearts be enlightened…” Not merely your minds. Your hearts. Paul seems to describe a kind of knowing deeper than information itself. Not irrationality, but a transformed perception of reality. And perhaps that is why he also prays for “a spirit of wisdom and revelation resulting in knowledge of Him.” This comes directly after the Ascension, as the disciples wait for the Holy Spirit. Almost as though humanity is moving into a new relationship with God: no longer dependent on physical sight alone.

Then the Gospel becomes even more precise. “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”
And I found myself stopping there. What is actually happening in baptism? Not symbolically. Not culturally. But truly. Because Christ does not speak about it casually. He speaks first from authority: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” Then comes the command to baptize. So baptism is not presented merely as a beautiful tradition, a public dedication, or emotional symbolism. It comes from the authority of the risen Christ Himself. And the language is exact:  “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”
 To baptize someone in His name is to place them into covenant, into belonging, into communion with the life of God. Almost as though something is being claimed over the person. A seal. An adoption. An entrance into divine life itself.

And perhaps this is why humanity responds to baptism the way it does. Even now, people instinctively become quiet during those moments. Conversations stop. Parents cry. People hold their breath without realizing it. Time itself almost feels interrupted. Not because everyone suddenly abandons reason. But because somewhere deep within human consciousness is the recognition that something real is occurring — something beyond performance, beyond psychology, beyond information alone. Almost as though our ordinary reality briefly opens toward another reality beyond it. The visible and invisible seem to touch: water, words, silence, eternity.

And perhaps this is what modern skepticism often misses. Christianity was never merely trying to explain electricity, disease, or gaps in scientific knowledge. It was trying to speak about the deepest realities human beings continue to encounter but cannot fully contain: this unconscious longing for eternity, the strange human awareness that existence itself feels unfinished.

To my son's point, did we invent God to fill in the gaps of missing knowledge?  Perhaps the deeper question is not whether humanity invented God to explain what it did not know.

But whether humanity keeps encountering something that knowledge alone cannot fully contain.
And in moments like baptism, whether one fully understands it or not, people seem to recognize that they are standing at the edge of something infinite — a moment where eternity does not merely symbolize itself through human ritual, but where, somehow, eternity itself reaches into time.
